messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Daniel Weber, a 35-year-old special education teacher, traced the start of his difficulties to an evening mugging eight months earlier. He had stayed late at school preparing individualized lesson materials and left carrying a backpack full of student files. On the walk to his car, a man came up behind him, shouted at him to hand everything over, and yanked him by the shoulder hard enough to wrench his neck. Daniel remembered seeing, almost frame by frame, the man’s mouth open in a yell, the angle of the parking lot lights, the pressure in his neck, and then the sudden arrival of police lights after it was over. What stayed with him most was not only fear but a hot, humiliating rage that he had been overpowered so quickly, mixed with guilt that he had been carrying school materials and had, in his mind, “put himself in that position” by leaving alone so late.

In the weeks that followed, those details did not soften. Daniel described the memory as if he were looking at still photographs laid out in front of him rather than remembering something finished and past. Certain moments in daily life pulled those images up immediately. If a student raised his voice sharply in the classroom, or if shouting echoed in the hallway, he was back in the parking lot for a second, seeing the mugger’s face and feeling the surge of rage and guilt that came with it. Neck pain was especially potent; if he turned too fast while helping a child and felt a twinge, the image of being grabbed returned with startling clarity. The sight of police near school dismissal could do the same. Even though he knew they were there for ordinary reasons, their presence called up the aftermath of the robbery so vividly that he would momentarily feel as if the event were happening again.

As Daniel tried to make sense of what had happened, he had come to believe it said something basic and damning about him. Somebody else, he thought, would not have gotten into this situation. A more capable man would have noticed danger earlier, reacted faster, fought back better. He spoke about himself as inadequate in a flat, convinced way. From that position, being constantly on guard felt necessary rather than excessive. He was certain he had to monitor everything because he was the kind of person things happened to. Even in safe places he could not relax; the conviction that he was vulnerable and insufficient kept his body braced, his attention fixed on possible threat, and his eyes moving automatically to exits the moment he entered any room or building.

Those same harsh conclusions also colored the way he remembered the mugging. When the scene came back to him, it did not come as a neutral replay. It arrived with self-accusation already attached: he saw the images and immediately judged himself against an imagined other person who would have handled it differently. The more inadequate he felt, the more guilt there was in the remembering, and the more the memory burned with rage at the mugger and at himself.

By the time he sought treatment, the sense of current danger and the memories were feeding each other tightly. Because he was so keyed up, any loud voice at school, any pull in his neck, any glimpse of a police officer in the parking lot was noticed instantly and felt loaded. That constant monitoring made the world seem full of reminders, and the reminders brought back the photographic flashes of the attack. Once that happened, he would feel himself jolt into the same state again—heart racing, body tight, unable to settle, scanning the classroom door and nearby exits as though he might need to move his students to safety. He hated that he sometimes became less available to the children when this happened; while a child was dysregulated and shouting, part of Daniel was managing the lesson and part of him was no longer fully in the room.

Over months, this pattern deepened his view of himself. Each episode in which he froze internally or stayed tense for hours afterward seemed to prove that he was inadequate and that other people would cope better. That belief, in turn, kept him watchful and unable to let down, which meant he noticed triggers even faster. He finally came for help after realizing he was organizing his entire workday around how to avoid being caught off guard, yet still having flashback-like moments in class. What frightened him most was the possibility that this was simply who he was now: a man who could not protect himself, could not relax, and could not be fully present for the students who depended on him. What he hoped, cautiously, was that he might learn how to walk into a room without first looking for the exits and without feeling the parking lot come rushing back.
